name: Rufinamide (Banzel)
summary: Antiseizure medication used for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. In psychiatry, it’s not a standard treatment—but it can still affect mood, energy, sleepiness, and behavior.
description: Rufinamide (Banzel) is an antiseizure medication used as add-on treatment for seizures in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS). It’s not a psychiatric medication, but it can cause CNS effects like drowsiness, fatigue, dizziness, attention problems, and (less commonly) anxiety or behavioral changes. It can also shorten the QT interval on ECG, so it’s not used in people with familial short QT syndrome. Always take it with food, and never stop it abruptly—stopping suddenly can increase seizure risk.
patient_summary: Rufinamide (Banzel) is mainly for seizures (Lennox-Gastaut syndrome), not anxiety or depression. But it can still impact how you feel day-to-day: sleepiness, fatigue, dizziness, and attention issues are common. Rarely, it can worsen mood or cause behavioral changes. It can also shorten the QT interval, so it’s not used in people with familial short QT syndrome. Take it with food and taper slowly if you ever need to stop.

primary_indications: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (adjunctive treatment of seizures) in adults and children 1 year and older

linked_conditions.context: FDA-labeled as adjunctive therapy for seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS).

contraindications: Canadian labeling (additional): Family history of short QT syndrome; presence or history of short QT interval; hypersensitivity to rufinamide, triazole derivatives, or any component of the formulation

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Extent decreases as dose increases; tablets and suspension are bioequivalent
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hydrolysis via carboxylesterase-mediated conversion to CGP 47292 (inactive metabolite); weak inducer of CYP3A4; weak inhibitor of CYP2E1
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food increases absorption; take with food

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Rufinamide (Banzel) is an antiseizure medication for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS). It is not a standard psychiatric medication for anxiety, panic, insomnia, agitation, or mood disorders.
items: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (adjunctive): Used alongside other antiseizure medications to reduce seizure burden

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This medication isn’t prescribed for psychiatric symptoms, but it can still affect mood, energy, and cognition. Here’s how people commonly describe it:

quotes: It helped my seizures, but I felt more wiped out during the day.
I was sleepy at first—like my brain was moving in slow motion.
Some days I had to plan around the fatigue.
items.note: Drowsiness and fatigue are common and can be dose-related.

quotes: My attention was kind of scattered for a while.
I felt off-balance and dizzy when we increased the dose.
I was more clumsy than usual—like my coordination was lagging.
items.note: Cognitive slowing, dizziness, ataxia, and gait changes can happen, especially during titration.

quotes: I got more irritable than I expected.
My anxiety popped up even though I wasn’t taking it for that.
My family noticed I was more on edge during dose changes.
items.note: Behavioral effects can occur, including anxiety (reported in adults) and aggression/activation (reported more in children). Any suicidal thoughts or major mood changes need urgent medical attention.

items.category: GI Side Effects (Can Affect Mood Too)
quotes: Nausea hit me on and off, especially if I didn’t eat enough.
It messed with my stomach at first, then settled down.
If I took it with food, it was way easier.
items.note: Taking rufinamide with food improves absorption and may help tolerability.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Rufinamide isn’t used for rapid psychiatric relief. For seizure management, it’s titrated up over days, and side effects can show up early—especially sleepiness, dizziness, and attention issues.
key_points: Take with food: Food increases absorption, which affects how strongly it hits
4-6 hours: Time to peak blood levels after a dose
6-10 hours: Half-life (how long it takes your body to clear about half the dose)
Early days of titration: Side effects like drowsiness/dizziness are often most noticeable

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Rufinamide is not a psychiatric medication and isn’t prescribed to treat anxiety, panic, insomnia, agitation, or mood disorders. Any mental-health-related changes are typically side effects (like sedation, fatigue, or behavioral shifts), not therapeutic targets.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: QT shortening risk + suicidality warning: this one needs respect.
other: Short QT risk: Rufinamide can shorten the QT interval and is contraindicated in familial short QT syndrome. Use caution with other QT-shortening medications.
CNS effects: Somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, coordination problems, and attention/cognitive effects can impair driving, work, and school functioning.

Serious hypersensitivity reactions (DRESS): Fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and organ involvement (eg, hepatitis, nephritis, myocarditis) require urgent evaluation and often discontinuation.
Serious skin reactions (including SJS): New or worsening rash should be treated as a medical priority.
Leukopenia: Decreased white blood cells can occur.
Suicidal thoughts/behavior: Antiseizure medications as a class are associated with a small increased risk; monitor closely, especially early in treatment.
Withdrawal: Do not stop abruptly unless there’s a safety emergency—abrupt discontinuation can increase seizure frequency.
patient_counseling: Take with food. It changes absorption and can change how strong the medication feels.
If you get extreme sleepiness, dizziness, falls, or confusion—tell your prescriber. Don’t “push through” it if it’s unsafe.
If you notice new depression, suicidal thoughts, intense agitation, or major behavior changes, treat it as urgent—call your clinician right away.
Rash + fever + swollen glands + feeling sick = don’t wait. That combo can signal a serious reaction (DRESS).
Don’t stop suddenly. If you need to come off, taper with your prescriber to reduce seizure rebound risk.
Avoid combining with other QT-shortening meds unless your clinician has specifically reviewed it.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: drowsiness, fatigue, dizziness, headache, and GI upset (especially nausea/vomiting). It can also affect coordination and attention. Rare but serious reactions include severe rash (SJS), DRESS, and blood count changes.
plain_language_list: Nausea or vomiting (more common in kids)
Trouble with attention or slower thinking

common.patient_note: This can feel like heavy eyelids, slowed thinking, and reduced motivation. It’s most noticeable early on or after dose increases. Don’t drive or do high-risk tasks until you know how you respond.
Fatigue can overlap with mood—when you’re exhausted, everything feels harder. If fatigue is crushing or persistent, dosing strategy and interactions should be reviewed.
This can show up as lightheadedness, motion sensitivity, or feeling unsteady. Falls are a real risk—especially in older adults or anyone with baseline balance issues.
Headaches can be part of the adjustment period. If severe, persistent, or associated with other red flags, it needs a closer look.
Taking it with food matters. If you’re vomiting doses, seizure control can destabilize, and side effects can snowball.
You may feel clumsy, off-balance, or “not synced up.” This is especially important if you’re also taking other sedating meds.
Some people notice irritability, anxiety, agitation, or behavioral activation—especially during titration. If there are suicidal thoughts or major mood shifts, treat it as urgent.

serious: Shortened QT interval and conduction changes: Can increase risk in susceptible individuals; contraindicated in familial short QT syndrome.

DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms): Fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and organ involvement (eg, hepatitis, nephritis, myocarditis). Potentially fatal—medical emergency.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS): Severe blistering rash and mucosal involvement—medical emergency.
Severe blood count problems (postmarketing): Agranulocytosis; also leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia reported.
Suicidal thoughts/behavior: Antiseizure medications as a class show a small increased risk; monitor closely, especially early treatment.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Rufinamide can interact with other medications, especially other antiseizure meds and hormone-based contraception. It’s also a weak inducer of CYP3A4, which can reduce levels of certain drugs metabolized through that pathway.

items.with: Other medications that shorten the QT interval
items.risk: Additive QT shortening could increase cardiac risk in susceptible patients.
items.action: Avoid the combo when possible, or use caution with ECG/clinical monitoring as directed by a clinician.

items.risk: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure meds can reduce contraceptive effectiveness; rufinamide has enzyme-inducing effects and may contribute to reduced reliability depending on regimen.
items.action: If pregnancy prevention matters, use a barrier method in addition to combined hormonal contraception, and review contraception options with a clinician.

items.risk: Significant interactions can exist requiring dose/frequency adjustment or avoidance.
items.action: Medication combinations should be reviewed carefully; monitoring of concurrent antiseizure drug levels may be needed.

items.risk: Food increases absorption, which can increase exposure and side effects if dosing isn’t consistent.
items.action: Take with food consistently (don’t alternate between fasting and heavy meals).

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Even though this isn’t a psychiatric medication, the discontinuation rule is the same: don’t stop abruptly unless there’s a safety emergency. Sudden discontinuation can increase seizure frequency. In trials, tapering by reducing the dose by about 25% every 2 days was effective.
key_points: Do not stop suddenly unless a serious reaction requires urgent discontinuation.
Goal: Minimize seizure rebound and destabilization.
Trial taper approach: Reduce total daily dose by ~25% every 2 days.
If you’re on multiple antiseizure meds, taper plans should account for interactions and overall seizure stability.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Rufinamide is not used for psychiatric indications like anxiety, panic, insomnia, agitation, or mood disorders. Dosing below is therefore not applicable in a psychiatry-focused context.

adult.not_applicable: Not applicable for this medication (no standard psychiatric indication).

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Rufinamide is an antiseizure medication, so special-population decisions usually balance seizure control against fetal/infant risk and medication tolerability. In psychiatry-focused care, the most relevant issues are sedation/cognition, mood changes, and suicidality monitoring—especially during medication changes.
sections.pregnancy: Data in humans are insufficient to clearly define risks of major congenital malformations or neurodevelopmental outcomes. Animal studies showed adverse effects. If a patient becomes pregnant while stable on an effective seizure regimen, changing meds can be risky—decisions should be individualized. Folic acid supplementation prior to and during pregnancy is recommended for patients on antiseizure medications. Encourage enrollment in the North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry (1-888-233-2334).
sections.lactation: It is not known if rufinamide is present in breast milk. If breastfeeding during therapy, monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding/sucking, weight gain, abnormal platelet counts, abnormal liver function, and developmental milestones.
sections.pediatrics: Approved for seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in children 1 year and older as adjunctive therapy. Children may experience behavioral effects more than adults (eg, aggression, attention disturbance, hyperactivity), and serious hypersensitivity reactions have been reported within the first 4 weeks in children under 12 in case reports.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing in general medical use. Initiate at the low end of the dosing range and use caution. From a mental-health standpoint, watch closely for sedation, falls, confusion, and cognitive slowing.
sections.hepatic: Mild to moderate impairment: Use with caution. Severe impairment: Not recommended (has not been studied).
sections.renal: Adult: No dosage adjustment provided in labeling; adjustment is unlikely based on pharmacokinetic evidence. Pediatric: CrCl <30 mL/min: No adjustment necessary. Hemodialysis: Dialyzable (~30%); consider dose adjustment for drug loss.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Sedation, fatigue, dizziness, and coordination: Especially during initiation and titration; assess fall risk and daily functioning.
Cognition and attention: Monitor for slowed thinking, attention problems, and school/work impairment, particularly in children and adolescents.
Mood and behavior: Watch for irritability, agitation, anxiety, aggression, and any suicidal thoughts or depression; monitor closely early in treatment and during dose changes.
Rash and systemic hypersensitivity: Monitor for rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and signs of organ involvement; evaluate immediately if suspected.
Cardiac conduction (QT interval): Be cautious in patients with QT-related concerns or when combined with QT-shortening medications; avoid in familial short QT syndrome.
Blood counts: Monitor for leukopenia and other hematologic abnormalities if clinically indicated or if symptoms suggest infection/bruising.
Concurrent antiseizure medication levels: Monitor serum levels of other antiseizure medications when clinically relevant due to interaction potential.
Nutrition/GI tolerability: Nausea/vomiting can disrupt adherence and destabilize seizure control; reinforce taking with food.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Rufinamide is available as tablets and an oral suspension. Dosing is typically split into two daily doses and taken with food for better absorption.
items: Oral suspension: 40 mg/mL (brand and generic available; shake well; measure with calibrated oral syringe)
Oral tablets: 200 mg, 400 mg (brand and generic; tablets may be swallowed whole, split, or crushed)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Rufinamide is a triazole-derivative antiseizure medication. Its exact mechanism isn’t fully known, but in vitro it appears to prolong the inactive state of sodium channels, which reduces repetitive firing of sodium-dependent action potentials. In plain terms: it helps calm overactive electrical firing in the brain that can drive seizures.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In a psychiatry-focused setting, rufinamide usually shows up because a patient has epilepsy (especially Lennox-Gastaut syndrome) and is taking it as part of seizure management. The clinical priority is coordination with neurology while monitoring for CNS side effects (sleepiness, fatigue, dizziness, cognitive slowing) and mental-health risks that can be relevant to any antiseizure medication—especially suicidality and behavioral changes. It is not used as a primary treatment for anxiety, insomnia, agitation, or mood disorders.

seo.title: Rufinamide (Banzel): Side Effects, Warnings, Interactions & What to Watch For
seo.description: Rufinamide (Banzel) is an antiseizure medication for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Psychiatry-relevant issues include drowsiness, fatigue, dizziness, attention changes, mood/behavior shifts, suicidality warning, QT shortening risk, serious rash/DRESS, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: Is rufinamide (Banzel) used for anxiety or insomnia?
faqs.a: No. Rufinamide is an antiseizure medication for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, not a psychiatric medication for anxiety, panic, insomnia, agitation, or mood disorders. If it affects how you feel mentally, it’s usually through side effects (like sleepiness, fatigue, dizziness, or attention problems), not because it’s treating a psychiatric condition.

faqs.q: Why does my prescriber care about mood or suicidal thoughts on an antiseizure medication?
faqs.a: Because antiseizure medications as a class carry a warning about a small increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior. It doesn’t mean it will happen—but it means you and your clinicians should take new depression, suicidal thoughts, or major behavior changes seriously, especially early in treatment or during dose changes.

faqs.q: What are the most common “mental” side effects?
faqs.a: The most common psychiatry-relevant effects are drowsiness, fatigue, dizziness, slowed thinking, attention problems, and coordination issues. Less commonly, people can experience anxiety, irritability, agitation, or behavioral changes.

faqs.q: What’s the QT warning and who should not take rufinamide?
faqs.a: Rufinamide can shorten the QT interval on an ECG. It is contraindicated in people with familial short QT syndrome. If you’re on other medications that also shorten QT, your clinician needs to review that combination carefully.

faqs.q: Can rufinamide cause serious allergic-type reactions?
faqs.a: Yes. Rarely, it can cause DRESS (a serious multi-organ hypersensitivity reaction) and severe skin reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS). Fever plus rash plus swollen glands or feeling systemically ill is not a “wait and see” situation—get evaluated urgently.

faqs.q: Do I really have to take it with food?
faqs.a: Yes—take rufinamide with food. Food increases absorption, which affects how much medication your body actually gets. Taking it inconsistently (sometimes fasting, sometimes with a big meal) can make side effects and seizure control harder to predict.

faqs.q: Can I stop rufinamide suddenly if I feel too sedated?
faqs.a: Don’t stop suddenly unless your clinician tells you to because of a serious safety concern. Abruptly stopping antiseizure medication can increase seizure frequency. If sedation is severe, contact your prescriber right away—there may be safer adjustments than stopping cold turkey.

faqs.q: How do people taper off rufinamide?
faqs.a: Tapering should be individualized, but in trials a taper of reducing the dose by about 25% every 2 days was effective. The key principle is gradual discontinuation to reduce the risk of seizure rebound—unless a serious reaction requires faster withdrawal.

faqs.q: Does rufinamide interact with birth control?
faqs.a: It can. Antiseizure medications with enzyme-inducing effects can reduce the effectiveness of certain hormonal contraceptives. If pregnancy prevention matters, a barrier method is often recommended in addition to combined hormonal contraception, and you should review options with your clinician.

faqs.q: Is rufinamide safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Human data are limited. If someone is stable on an effective seizure regimen, changing meds during pregnancy can be risky, so decisions are individualized. Folic acid supplementation is recommended for people who could become pregnant while taking antiseizure medications. It’s not known if rufinamide passes into breast milk; if breastfeeding during therapy, infants should be monitored for sedation, feeding issues, weight gain, labs (platelets/liver function), and developmental milestones.
